analysis.title: Global Strategy Weekly: Red screens: Why is (almost) no-one talking about liquidity?
key_insights: Albert Edwards argues that tightening liquidity is a main driver of the recent post-mid-term-election tech slump. He says none of the explanations he read mentioned it.

He cites Michael Howell's liquidity work and Simon White (Bloomberg), who measures liquidity as money supply in excess of nominal GDP growth. White wrote in June, as the Nasdaq was topping out, that the liquidity squeeze was just getting started.

Edwards says macro narratives are often invented after the event to explain moves that are really driven by rising or falling liquidity. If the tide is going out, he advises not fixating on macro or stock-specific factors.

White's 5 Nov piece says the liquidity squeeze is a problem for the AI trade, which is already under pressure from concerns about capex levels and compute overcapacity. Semis are the sector most positively sensitive to the yield curve, followed by energy.

Forward EPS growth for US IT and the S&P 500 is still strong, but both lines have decelerated recently. The breadth of analyst EPS upgrades has also slowed, and the change in IT EPS upgrades has turned down ahead of the equity market. Edwards concludes the slump may not be only liquidity related.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said at Jackson Hole that he watches the second derivative of profits growth. Profit growth is slowing while October core CPI came in stronger than expected.
Core CPI measures look benign on a yoy basis. Core CPI ex shelter has been near 2.0% for three years. The October 2025 CPI data is missing and was interpolated to get the October 2026 yoy rate.
The recent 3-month annualised rise in key core CPI measures is more worrying, and core CPI ex shelter and used cars is worse still. Edwards says one more 0.3% mom rise would be a problem.

The Q3 productivity report confirmed that the Q2 surge in corporate output prices above 4% was not a one-off. Edwards notes this series often leads core CPI and core PCE, and big moves up are almost always followed by a surge in core inflation.
Edwards is concerned that October's hot core CPI is the start of a trend. He asks rhetorically whether anyone is ready for Fed hikes of 200bp or more.
Edwards says he has heard that the AI boom is different in every bubble, and that each collapse surprised the bulls. He calls the current market an AI investment bubble.

sector_views.rationale: Semis are the sector most positively sensitive to the yield curve, so a liquidity squeeze is a particular vulnerability. The sector is also facing concerns about capex and compute overcapacity (view cited from Simon White, endorsed by Edwards).
Energy is the only other sector with a positive relationship to the yield curve over this horizon, per White. No explicit call is made.

risk_factors: Tightening liquidity, measured as money supply growth relative to nominal GDP growth, hurting risk assets.
Semis' sensitivity to the yield curve during a liquidity squeeze.
Concerns about AI capex levels and compute overcapacity.
Slowing EPS upgrades and slowing forward profit growth.
Re-acceleration of core CPI and core PCE, with a possible Fed response of large rate hikes.

tension_points.bull_case: Profit forecasts are still booming, with strong forward EPS growth for US IT and the S&P 500.
tension_points.bear_case: Liquidity is tightening and EPS growth and upgrade breadth are decelerating. Semis are sensitive to the yield curve, and concerns about capex and compute overcapacity add to the risk. Edwards calls the AI boom a bubble.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Edwards says the 3-month annualised core CPI ex shelter rate needs to turn down soon. Another 0.3% mom core CPI rise would support the bear case.

theme_stances.key_argument: Liquidity makes the weather for markets, and the recent tech slump was likely driven by a deteriorating liquidity situation.
Higher corporate output prices and a rising 3-month core CPI rate suggest October's hot core CPI may be the start of a trend.
